claims.claim: I.1 and I.2 are of two distinct types: I.1 a stretto fugue without episodes (real answer, free counterpoint, subject in almost every bar, nearly always in stretto after the exposition); I.2 an episodic fugue without stretto (tonal answer, countersubject, entries separated by episodes).
Most fugues tend to be of one or the other type, though stretto and episodic principles are not necessarily opposed: some fugues effectively blend both.

Common features of I.1 and I.2: single-voice opening; imitative entries at dominant or tonic pitch; later entries incl. at least one in a key other than I/V; return to tonic toward the end; coda on tonic pedal.

Definitions: answer = first entry of second voice at dominant pitch; codetta = short connecting passage between entries; countersubject = secondary theme accompanying the answer and recurring; redundant entry = extra entry after the exposition in tonic or dominant before modulating; counterexposition = second set of entries in all voices, usually in I/V, often in opposite subject/answer order; episode = passage between entries, figure development, often modulating; stretto = overlapping of entries; coda = rounding-off passage, often on a tonic pedal.
A fugue is defined by style rather than form (quotes Benjamin and Vaughan Williams).

claims.claim: Groups 1 and 2 have more than seventy episodes; episodes occupy from one-third to two-thirds of a fugue (see Appendix A).
All episodes develop thematic material (subject, CS, codetta); new figures subordinate; some melodic sequence virtually a necessity.
Less frequent progressions: roots falling a third and rising a second; rising a second and falling a fifth; falling a third. In rising sequences: roots rising a fourth and falling a third.
About four in five of the sequences are falling sequences on roots falling a fifth and rising a fourth.
claims.note: cf. p.28: falling fifths in almost three-quarters of all 200+ episodes of the 48

claims.claim: With only two episodes, the second is normally a development or interchanged restatement of the first; with more, partial contrast more common than complete contrast.
Episodes are the chief means of modulation; they both separate and join entries (dovetailing).

intro.claim: In Group 3 stretto becomes an element of formal organization; episodes may be fewer and of secondary importance. Orders: middle-soprano-bass 3, soprano-middle-bass 3, bass-soprano-middle 1.

general.claim: Stretto is not a "device" applicable to any subject: only to subjects designed for it or found to have the possibility (unlike inversion, augmentation, diminution).
Most stretto fugues start with an orthodox exposition before revealing stretto possibilities.

claims.claim: Bach prefers cyclic order even in keyboard fugues and avoids soprano-middle-bass descending order in four-part fugues.
After the exposition a four-part fugue does not differ basically from a three-part one; texture reduced to three or two voices, four reserved for climaxes.
